Locate unresolved shoulders within a peak

dot-peak_shoulders.Rd

Locate unresolved shoulders within a peak

Usage

.peak_shoulders(
  y,
  rt,
  apex,
  start,
  end,
  depth_frac = 0.02,
  width_frac = 0.18,
  noise = 0,
  noise_k = c(10, 5),
  slide_sigma = 3,
  min_height = 0
)

Arguments

y

Numeric vector; smoothed, baseline-corrected signal.

rt

Numeric vector of times, same length as y.

apex, start, end

Integer indices of the peak apex and bounds in y.

depth_frac

Numeric; a second-derivative dip must have a prominence of at least this fraction of the apex's second-derivative depth.

width_frac

Numeric; second-derivative filter length as a fraction of the peak width in points (adapts to peak width and sampling rate).

noise

Numeric; white-noise SD of the unsmoothed signal. The dip prominence must also reach a sliding multiple of the noise propagated through the second-derivative filter (see Details). 0 disables the noise gate.

noise_k

Numeric length 2; noise multiples at the apex and on the flank (from slide_sigma peak sigmas outward).

slide_sigma

Numeric; distance from the apex, in peak sigmas, over which the multiple falls linearly from noise_k[1] to noise_k[2].

min_height

Numeric; minimum signal height at a shoulder.

Value

Integer vector (possibly empty, sorted) of indices into y of second-derivative dips inside the peak that are not explained by the apex. Each marks an unresolved overlapping component.

Details

A dip is a local minimum of the second derivative, measured by its prominence (depth below the lower flanking maximum) rather than by its sign, so a small component on the flank of a larger peak, where the second derivative is positive, is still found. On synthetic Gaussians at moderate noise, a 10% component 3 sigma from the apex is reliably found; 5% components, or components 2.5 sigma or less away, generally are not: their dips are no larger than noise dips.

The noise gate slides with distance from the apex. Peak sigma is estimated from the full width at half maximum (FWHM / 2.355) of y. A dip d sigmas from the apex must reach k(d) = noise_k[1] + (noise_k[2] - noise_k[1]) * min(d / slide_sigma, 1) times the second-derivative noise. Ragged or flat tops near the apex are held to a stricter standard than flank shoulders, where real minor components appear.
